new_statements.quote: The sign ¯ represents the long sound, and ˘ the short one. Thus 'abat' = our 'ah! but'; and 'abut' = our 'a boot'; the sign ' shows where the accentuation falls. [p. ix] ... With few exceptions the nouns (and other parts of speech) are monosyllabic, and, though this is so, it may be said that intonation is not a feature of the language. 2. If a noun has several meanings, these are not differentiated by tones, but by tacking on another word with a meaning similar to the one required. [p. 1] ... in a-ji -be-ni, and a-ji mi-ni, the accent is on ji. [p. 245]
new_statements.citation: Foulkes, H. D. (1915). Angass Manual: Grammar and Vocabulary. London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner.
new_statements.locator: p. ix, 'Explanation of diacritical marks' (archive.org leaf 14); and Grammar ch. I par. 1-2, p. 1 (leaf 24); vocabulary notes p. 245 s.v. mini and p. 264 s.v. pil
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated: Foulkes marks 'accentuation' lexically with an acute sign on individual (mostly monosyllabic) words and phrases, and explicitly denies that the language has tone. Every later description (Burquest 1971 via PHOIBLE; Jungraithmayr & Holubová 2016 via Tourneux 2016) treats Ngas as a three-register tone language with lexical and demarcative tone, so Foulkes's acute marks are best read as high-tone marks, not word stress. No modern source that was opened says anything about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; two vocabulary notes give phrase-level prominence ('the accent is on ji' in the imperative phrase a-ji mi-ni 'come here', p. 245; 'heavy accent on the pil' for the emphatic particle, p. 264).
new_statements.domain_note: Notational statement covers words in the vocabulary; the two explicit accent remarks are about phrases (imperative + locative; emphatic particle). Words are overwhelmingly monosyllabic (Foulkes p. 1; Tourneux 2016 on Jungraithmayr & Holubová), so a word-stress rule would be nearly vacuous.
new_statements.identity_note: Foulkes 1915 describes 'Plain Angass' of the Pankshin/Ampang area and contrasts Hill vs Plain dialects (p. vi: Hill ka vs Plain ke 'head'); Ormsby 1913-14 gives the autonym Karang; Jungraithmayr 1964 is the Angas of Kabwir (Hill), Jungraithmayr & Holubová 2016 is 'Shik Ngas'. All are the Glottolog language ngas1240 (ISO anc); no separate dialect glottocodes were checked.

sources.note: No phonology chapter; only an 'Explanation of diacritical marks' (p. ix, IA leaf 14): 'the sign ' shows where the accentuation falls' -- accent is marked word by word with an acute sign, no placement rule is given. Grammar p. 1 par. 1-2 claims 'intonation is not a feature of the language' and that homonyms are 'not differentiated by tones' (refuted by all later work; Ngas has three tone registers). sources.citation: Tourneux, Henri (2016). Review of Jungraithmayr & Holubová 2016, The Ngas Language (Shik Ngas). Journal des africanistes 86-2: 235-237. DOI 10.4000/africanistes.5147
sources.note: Summarises the book's phonology sketch second-hand: 61 consonants (25 basic), 6 short + 6 long vowels, 'On a trois registres tonals (H, B, M) et les tons ponctuels et modulés qui en découlent. Le ton a une fonction lexicale et démarcative.' Most lexemes monosyllabic CVC/CVVC. No mention of stress or accent d'intensité.

sources.citation: Ormsby, George (1913-1914). Some Notes on the Angass Language. Journal of the African Society 12(48): 421-424; 13(49): 54-61; 13(50): 204-210; 13(51): 316-321.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Editor's preface p. 421: 'No phonetic analysis was supplied by the author'; a final 'h' in the author's spelling ('Either a rise of tone was intended, or the preceding vowel was considered to be more tense') is re-marked 'by an acute accent over the preceding vowel'. Editor's footnote p. 204: 'Probably Angass distinguishes words by Intonation, as all other members of the Negro group do.'
